title: Lagos. Report for 1900–1901. Colonial Reports—Annual No. 348
publisher: Colonial Office / HMSO, 1902. University of Illinois Library digital copy.
locator: Printed pp. 3–4, Blue Book transmittal and Revenue and Expenditure. The population denominator is printed on p. 4.
rights: Historical population facts and bibliographic references only. No scans or prose reproduced.
date_note: The report names financial year 1900–1901. The Colonial Secretary signed the report on 5 November 1901. The population paragraph gives no reference day or calculation method.
boundary_note: The denominator covers the combined Colony and Protectorate of Lagos. The Lagos administration remained separate at the Royal Niger Company handover. The Southern Nigeria Order identifies Akure as belonging to Lagos and Ikaha and its dependencies as belonging to Southern Nigeria. The CShapes Lagos geometry includes Abeokuta, where Britain signed the 1893 treaty conditionally recognizing Egba independence. The contemporary population sources do not state whether Abeokuta or the rest of Egba country was included in the whole-jurisdiction estimate or the 1901 Western District estimate. Neither return supplies a district population crosswalk for the opening-date polygon.

references.locator: Colonial Reports—Annual No. 321, Lagos, 1899, printed p. 21, section VII, paragraph 49. The report gives no population estimate because the last census was in 1891.
House of Commons, 3 July 1899, cols. 1298–1299. The proposed company-territory division preserves the existing Lagos administration.
J. A. O. Payne, Table of Principal Events in Yoruba History, printed p. 107, text of the Treaty of Friendship and Commerce made at Abeokuta on 18 January 1893, article 5.
House of Commons, 16 March 1908, Treaty with the Egba Chiefs. The Colonial Under-Secretary confirmed recognition of conditional Egba independence.

title: Census of the British Empire, 1901. Lagos and Nigeria entries and explanatory notes
publisher: General Register Office / HMSO, 1906. Wellcome Collection digital copy.
locator: Printed pp. 4–5, Summary Table 2, Lagos and Nigeria entries and note (b); p. 145, section 18, table 1 and its footnote; p. 146, section 19, Nigeria.
rights: Wellcome Collection marks its digital copy Public Domain Mark 1.0. Historical population facts and bibliographic references only.
date_note: The Lagos section refers to 1901. The superintendent's rounded whole-territory alternative has no separate reference day. The northern and southern estimates supply no common census day. The p. 4 summary's 20,000,000 for Northern Nigeria is the upper endpoint of the range stated on p. 146.
boundary_note: Lagos Colony and Protectorate total 1,388,847, comprising 39,354 enumerated in Lagos Island and Harbour, 2,493 enumerated in Ebute Metta, and 1,347,000 estimated in seven inland or coastal districts and provinces. The superintendent considered overestimation more likely and gave 1,250,000 as an alternative for the whole jurisdiction. The published table, its seven district estimates and the northern and southern estimates already appear in collections/eastern. The empire table reports approximate areas of 26,700 square miles for combined Lagos, 49,704 for Southern Nigeria and 323,000 for Northern Nigeria. Those convert to approximately 69,153, 128,733 and 836,566 square kilometres. The WWO CShapes snapshot of 1900-03-12 reports respectively 71,584.9, 130,337 and 727,266 square kilometres for cshapes_gw_4781, cshapes_gw_4783 and cshapes_gw_4784. The northern difference is about 109,300 square kilometres. The difference does not identify which people or localities would be removed by a boundary adjustment.

references.locator: Wellcome IIIF manifest for the original volume. Use the canvases for printed pp. 4, 5, 145 and 146.
Colonial Reports—Annual No. 400, Lagos, 1902, printed pp. 29–30, Population. The official annual return reproduces the 1901 split between 41,847 enumerated and 1,347,000 estimated.

CShapes dataset. WWO uses the 1900-03-12 extract in data/world_map/historical/cshapes_1900_snapshot.json. The source geometries label both protectorates as starting 1899-01-01. The Orders took effect a year later.

title: Lagos. Report for 1903. Colonial Reports—Annual
publisher: Colonial Office / HMSO. University of Illinois Library digital copy.
rights: Historical population facts and bibliographic references only. No scans or prose reproduced.
date_note: 1903 is the report year. The denominator has no separate population reference day. The five-year period in the paragraph refers to liquor imports, with one population estimate used for comparison.
boundary_note: The denominator is expressly for the Lagos territory. The text gives no territorial components or population estimation method.

title: Southern Nigeria Order in Council, 1899, and the first annual returns for the protectorates
publisher: Privy Council and Colonial Office / HMSO.
locator: Edinburgh Gazette, 9 January 1900, printed p. 25, preamble and article II. See the annual reports for the effective date and statistical coverage.
rights: Historical and bibliographic facts only. No scans or prose reproduced.
date_note: The transfer took effect on 1 January 1900. On that date the original Niger Coast Protectorate and the southern part of Royal Niger Company territory became Southern Nigeria. The northern company territories became Northern Nigeria. The Niger Coast Protectorate's transfer to the Colonial Office on 1 April 1899 was a separate administrative change.
boundary_note: Article II of the Southern Nigeria Order traces the Río del Rey, Cross River rapids, a line towards Yola, and the northern boundary to Idda and Owo. It places Idda and Ikaha in Southern Nigeria, Takum north of the line, and Akure in Lagos. The southwestern boundary continues through the Lagos Creek and Arogbo to the coast, leaving the King of Mahin's territory west of the line. The Northern and Southern reports do not supply matching all-resident totals for these administrative extents at the handover. The source texts distinguish nominal protected territory from areas directly administered.

references.locator: Southern Nigeria annual report for 1899–1900, printed pp. 4 and 24, Royal Niger Company transfer and Order promulgation on 1 January 1900. Printed p. 17, section VII(A), gives average European presence of 270 over the reporting year and says the Indigenous population cannot be estimated.

Colonial Reports—Annual No. 289, Niger Coast Protectorate, 1898–99, printed p. 10. The predecessor return covers an average of 227 Europeans, 204 male and 23 female. The reporting areas changed at the transfer.
Colonial Reports—Annual No. 346, Northern Nigeria, report for 1 January 1900 to 31 March 1901. The first report contains no whole-protectorate population count.

Colonial Reports—Annual No. 1335, Nigeria, 1926, printed p. 4, paragraphs 5–7, and p. 5, paragraphs 8–9. The official retrospective distinguishes legal succession from the reach of effective administration.

Nigeria's written submissions in Land and Maritime Boundary between Cameroon and Nigeria, paragraph 6.68(5)–(7). Identifies both 1899 Orders and the 1 January 1900 effective date, citing London Gazette, 5 January 1900, pp. 69–73.

title: Federico–Tena World Population Historical Database: Nigeria reconstruction and colonial territorial coverage
publisher: e-cienciaDatos / Universidad Carlos III de Madrid.
locator: V5 List of Polities, Country series!AG103 and AG104. Methods working paper, printed pp. 9–11, and Appendix I, p. 52, Nigeria.
rights: CC BY 4.0, Giovanni Federico and Antonio Tena-Junguito. WWO extracts and interpolates historical population facts.
boundary_note: The historical-border workbook supplies one Nigeria series. The methods project sub-Saharan colonial series backward and give a single Nigeria entry without a three-way allocation. The WWO reconstruction is 19,081,911 at 1900-01-01. Subtracting the Lagos 1,500,000 fiscal estimate gives 17,581,911; also subtracting the Southern 5,000,000 estimate gives 12,581,911. Those arithmetic differences mix periods and estimation methods, with no verified match between the later colonial Nigerian territory and the 1900 statutory areas. They cannot serve as separate Northern Nigeria population observations. The WWO v7 opening has none of these three jurisdictions or an opening aggregate for Nigeria.

references.locator: 2025 methods working paper, section 4.1 and Appendix I, p. 52. The report identifies the use of area growth rates and later Frankema–Jerven polity-specific rates.
V5 workbook. Both nominal July values used in the opening interpolation refer to the same undivided Nigeria series.
